paragraphs.title: Complacency, Pride, and Suppressing the Day of Calamity

answers: Those who are at ease in Zion and trust in Samaria
The people of Gath only
Those who carry out the bones
easy.explanation: Amos addresses those at ease in Zion and those who trust in the mountain of Samaria.
easy.q: Whom does Amos condemn at the beginning of the passage?

answers: Prayer alone
Power, prosperity, and a sense of superiority
A life of poverty
easy.explanation: Their confidence rests on status, strength, prosperity, and national pride.
easy.q: What supports the confidence of the people described?

answers: The evil day
Their banquets
Their music
easy.explanation: They put far away the evil day instead of facing the coming judgment.
easy.q: What do they put far away?

answers: They bring the evil day closer
They ignore or postpone thinking about the evil day
They celebrate the evil day
medium.explanation: The phrase describes their denial and suppression of coming calamity.
medium.q: What does “put far away the evil day” mean in this context?

answers: To compare their strength and borders with those of Israel
To describe a commercial journey
To teach about musical instruments
medium.explanation: The comparison challenges their pride and confidence in their national position.
medium.q: Why does Amos mention Calneh, Hamath, and Gath?

answers: It leads them to tolerate or bring near violence
It causes them to leave their cities
It causes them to stop eating
medium.explanation: While putting away the evil day, they bring near the seat of violence.
medium.q: How is complacency connected with verse 3?

answers: Confidence and security versus approaching danger
Music versus silence
Poverty versus work
challenge.explanation: The people feel secure, but Amos warns that calamity is near.
challenge.q: What is the central contrast in the passage?

answers: They do not consider themselves special
They judge their status with pride and superiority
They want to learn agriculture from them
challenge.explanation: Their comparison with other kingdoms exposes their national arrogance.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the comparison with other kingdoms?

answers: Pride blinds them to danger and allows violence
Pride makes them care for the weak
Pride causes them to surrender their power
challenge.explanation: Their pride produces both denial of judgment and acceptance of violence.
challenge.q: What connection is shown between national pride and injustice?

paragraphs.title: Luxury and Indifference to Israel's Ruin

answers: Beds of ivory
Stones
Simple wooden benches
easy.explanation: The passage says that they lie upon beds of ivory.
easy.q: What do the people described lie upon?

answers: Bread and water only
Lambs, calves, wine, and chief ointments
Fruit only
easy.explanation: The verses describe rich food, wine, and costly ointments.
easy.q: What do they eat and drink?

answers: They will remain in their palaces
They will go captive with the first that go captive
They will receive new borders
easy.explanation: They will be taken into exile with the first captives.
easy.q: What will happen to them according to verse 7?

answers: They do not mourn or care about Israel's suffering
They care for the wounded
They go out to war
medium.explanation: The phrase shows their indifference to the affliction of Israel.
medium.q: What does “they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” mean?

answers: They all describe luxury and indulgence
They describe preparations for war
They describe a life of mourning
medium.explanation: Together, these details portray an extravagant and self-indulgent lifestyle.
medium.q: What do the beds, food, music, wine, and ointments have in common?

answers: They enjoyed luxury while ignoring Israel's suffering
They avoided every banquet
They worked in the fields
medium.explanation: The prophet connects their indulgence and indifference with coming exile.
medium.q: Why is exile presented as the result of their lifestyle?

answers: The contrast between private pleasure and Israel's affliction
The contrast between summer and winter
The contrast between musicians and farmers
challenge.explanation: The problem is not merely wealth, but enjoying it while ignoring national suffering.
challenge.q: What creates the strongest criticism in the passage?

answers: Their music is part of a life of idleness and indulgence
They do not know how to play
They do not use instruments
challenge.explanation: Their music accompanies luxury and indifference rather than faithful service.
challenge.q: Why does playing music “like David” not make these people positive figures?

answers: Luxury and indifference, followed by exile
Exile, followed by a banquet, and then security
War, followed by palace building, and finally music
challenge.explanation: The passage first describes their indulgence and indifference, then announces their exile.
challenge.q: What is the main sequence of ideas in the passage?

paragraphs.title: Destruction and Death Within the Houses

answers: The excellency of Jacob
The music
The border of Hamath
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces.”
easy.q: What does the Lord GOD abhor according to verse 8?

answers: They will be delivered to enemies
They will become larger
They will immediately be rebuilt
easy.explanation: God says, “I will deliver up the city with all that is therein.”
easy.q: What will happen to the city and all that is in it?

answers: They will die
They will flee into the wilderness
They will build a palace
easy.explanation: The verse states that if ten men remain in one house, they shall die.
easy.q: What will happen to the ten men remaining in one house?

answers: The city and its inhabitants will be handed over to enemies
The city will close for a celebration
The city will leave the land
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the city's surrender to destruction and its enemies.
medium.q: What does “I will deliver up the city with all that is therein” mean?

answers: The destruction will be very extensive
The houses will remain untouched
Death will occur only outside the city
medium.explanation: Many deaths within one house emphasize the scale of the disaster.
medium.q: What does the death of ten men in one house show about the destruction?

answers: Pride leads to the city's surrender, followed by death and broken houses
Music leads to the building of houses
Wealth leads to the city's rescue
medium.explanation: The passage moves from pride and judgment to death and physical destruction.

answers: It emphasizes an atmosphere of terror and silence
It invites everyone to a banquet
It encourages singing
challenge.explanation: The command to be silent intensifies the fearful mood surrounding the destruction.
challenge.q: Why does “Hold thy tongue” appear in the description of death?

answers: Destruction reaches both centers of wealth and ordinary houses
The palaces are spared while only houses suffer
The houses become places of celebration
challenge.explanation: The Lord's judgment reaches the entire city and its structures.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the movement from palaces to broken houses?

answers: The depth of death and desolation within the house
The prosperity of the family
The preparation of a meal
challenge.explanation: The bones represent the extensive death and ruin left inside the house.
challenge.q: What does the image of carrying out the bones emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Justice Turned into Injustice and Punishment by Conquest

answers: Horses running upon rock and oxen plowing there
Playing music on a viol
Drinking from bowls
easy.explanation: Amos asks whether horses can run upon rock or oxen plow there.
easy.q: What situation is pictured by the questions in verse 12?

answers: Gall and hemlock
Water and bread
Gold and oil
easy.explanation: They have turned judgment into gall and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock.
easy.q: What have Israel turned judgment and righteousness into?

answers: A nation that will afflict them
A city that will protect them
A kingdom that will enrich them
easy.explanation: The Lord will raise up a nation to afflict the house of Israel.
easy.q: What will the Lord raise up against Israel?

answers: Bitterness and poison
Joy
Wealth
medium.explanation: Hemlock represents the bitter and poisonous result of corrupted righteousness.
medium.q: What does “hemlock” symbolize in “the fruit of righteousness into hemlock”?

answers: Injustice prevents society from producing righteousness
Rock symbolizes abundance
Rock is ideal for growing crops
medium.explanation: As rocky ground cannot be properly plowed, injustice prevents a society from producing righteousness.
medium.q: Why is the image of rock appropriate for Amos's criticism of society?

answers: Their supposed strength will not prevent conquest and oppression
Their strength will bring them peace
Their strength will abolish judgment
medium.explanation: Although they boast in their power, the Lord will raise up a nation against them.
medium.q: What is the connection between their pride in strength and their punishment?

answers: The situation is abnormal and contrary to the proper order
Agriculture is flourishing
The horses are meant only for war
challenge.explanation: The questions highlight the impossibility and corruption of the social situation.
challenge.q: What do the rhetorical questions about rock, horses, and oxen show?

answers: Social injustice brings national judgment upon them
Corrupted justice protects them from enemies
Conquest prevents them from having any connection with justice
challenge.explanation: The injustice is presented as the setting for God's punishment through conquest.
challenge.q: How is corrupted justice connected with conquest?

answers: The oppression will extend from one end of the land to the other
The oppression will remain inside one house
The oppression will affect only the palaces
challenge.explanation: The expression describes the broad extent of the coming oppression across the land.
challenge.q: What does “from the entering in of Hemath unto the river of the wilderness” mean in context?
